--- title: "Take-home Exercise 1" subtitle: "Visual Analytics for Insurance Portfolio Profitability & Volatility" author: "Meng Tingyu" date: "2026-05-23" date-modified: "2026-05-23" format: html: code-fold: show code-tools: false code-summary: "Show code" code-line-numbers: false toc: true toc-depth: 3 toc-location: right number-sections: true fig-width: 10 fig-height: 6 fig-align: center fig-cap-location: bottom tbl-cap-location: top theme: [cosmo, custom.scss] css: custom.css smooth-scroll: true embed-resources: false execute: warning: false message: false freeze: auto cache: true editor: visual --- # Overview {.unnumbered} > *"Insurers often carry underperforming portfolios where the root causes of poor profitability and high volatility are unknown. Leveraging visual analytics can potentially help investigate trends in underlying loss drivers."* This study applies a **visual-analytics workflow** to a real-world Spanish motor-insurance portfolio (354,140 records over 2022–2024) to discover the drivers of **profitability** and **volatility**. Rather than producing yet another dashboard, the analysis combines univariate exploration, bivariate hypothesis-testing, and interactive cross-filtering to surface non-obvious portfolio dynamics that direct downstream underwriting decisions. ::: callout-note ## Working definitions **Profitability** is operationalised as the **Loss Ratio** (`LR = total_incurred / total_premium`). Values \< 1 indicate the premium covers claims; \> 1 indicates underwriting loss. We complement LR with **Pure Premium** (loss per unit exposure), **Claim Frequency** (claims per unit exposure) and **Severity** (cost per claim). **Volatility** is operationalised through three lenses: \(i\) the **coefficient of variation** of policy-level LR within each segment; \(ii\) **tail concentration**: the share of total losses generated by the largest claims (Lorenz/Gini); \(iii\) the **dispersion of severity** within segments. ::: # Analytical Workflow ```{mermaid} %%| fig-cap: "Analytical workflow from raw policy data to actionable insight." flowchart LR A[Raw CSV
354k rows · 47 cols
; delimiter] --> B[Data Wrangling
tidyverse] B --> C[Analytical Sandbox
+ derived KPIs] C --> D1[Univariate EDA
Numerical] C --> D2[Univariate EDA
Categorical] D1 --> E[Bivariate Analysis
+ Statistical Validation] D2 --> E E --> F1[Profitability Drivers] E --> F2[Volatility & Tail Risk] F1 --> G[Interactive
Cross-filtering
plotly · ggiraph] F2 --> G G --> H[Underwriting
Insight] style A fill:#f5f5f5,stroke:#333333,stroke-width:1px style C fill:#fafafa,stroke:#222222,stroke-width:1.5px style G fill:#ffffff,stroke:#000000,stroke-width:2px style H fill:#222222,stroke:#000000,color:#ffffff ``` # Data & Methodology ## Data source The dataset is a real-world motor-vehicle insurance portfolio published by a Spanish non-life insurer on [Mendeley Data](https://data.mendeley.com/). It contains **354,140 policy-year records** for **185,678 unique policies** across calendar years **2022, 2023 and 2024**, with 47 variables grouped into: - **Policy & insured** (8 vars): `policy_type`, `policy_status`, `business_type`, `payment_frequency`, `bonus_score`, etc. - **Driver & vehicle** (10 vars): `driver_age`, `vehicle_age`, `fuel_type`, `vehicle_value`, `vehicle_brand`, `municipality_type`, `circulation_area`, … - **Premiums** (8 vars): `total_premium` and 7 coverage-level premiums. - **Claim counts** (10 vars): `total_claims` plus per-coverage counts. - **Incurred losses** (10 vars): `total_incurred` plus per-coverage losses. - **Exposure** (2 vars): policy-year exposure used to annualise frequencies. ::: callout-warning ## Cookbook inconsistency identified The cookbook describes `age_driving_licence` as *"Year in which the insured obtained the driving licence"*, but the observed range is **0–80** with a sample like `{26, 19, 19, 18, 19}`. The variable is in fact the **number of years the licence has been held**. We treat it as years-held throughout this study and rename it `years_licence_held` in the sandbox to prevent downstream confusion. ::: ## Software stack ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} pacman::p_load( # Core tidyverse, lubridate, scales, knitr, kableExtra, # ggplot2 extensions ggridges, ggdist, ggrepel, ggstatsplot, ggcorrplot, ggpubr, patchwork, ggh4x, ggtext, # Interactive plotly, ggiraph, crosstalk, DT, # Statistics performance, FSA ) ``` ::: # Data Wrangling ## Import The raw file uses **semicolons** as field delimiter and **periods** as decimal mark (European convention). We use `readr::read_delim()` to handle this and explicitly type the columns to avoid `readr`'s heuristics misclassifying e.g. `insured_id` as numeric. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} raw_path <- "data/insurance_raw.csv" # Auto-detect delimiter: original Mendeley file is `;`-separated, but the # project copy may already be comma-normalised. We probe and pick. first_line <- readr::read_lines(raw_path, n_max = 1) delim <- if (stringr::str_detect(first_line, ";")) ";" else "," raw_df <- readr::read_delim( raw_path, delim = delim, locale = readr::locale(decimal_mark = ".", grouping_mark = ""), show_col_types = FALSE ) dim(raw_df) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 354140 47 ``` ::: ::: ## Audit A compact data-quality audit before any transformation. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} audit_tbl <- raw_df |> summarise(across( everything(), list( n_missing = ~sum(is.na(.x)), pct_missing = ~mean(is.na(.x)) * 100, n_unique = ~dplyr::n_distinct(.x) ), .names = "{.col}__{.fn}" )) |> tidyr::pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = c("variable", "metric"), names_sep = "__") |> tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = metric, values_from = value) |> arrange(desc(pct_missing)) audit_tbl |> filter(pct_missing > 0 | n_unique <= 10) |> knitr::kable( digits = 3, caption = "Variables with missingness or low cardinality", col.names = c("Variable", "Missing (n)", "Missing (%)", "Unique values") ) |> kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

````` ::: ::: **Findings**: - Missingness is negligible: `fuel_type` (0.36%), `vehicle_value` (0.14%), `vehicle_age` (\<0.001%). - 49 records have `total_premium = 0` **and** `total_exposure = 0`, these are inactive shells and must be removed. - `policy_status` has only two levels (A/C); `business_type` two (NB/P); `bonus_score` three (G/N/B). ## Cleaning & derivation ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sandbox <- raw_df |> # 1) rename the misleading cookbook variable rename(years_licence_held = age_driving_licence) |> # 2) drop inactive shells (0 premium & 0 exposure) filter(!(total_premium == 0 & total_exposure == 0)) |> # 3) impute the trivial missingness with category "Unknown" mutate( fuel_type = forcats::fct_na_value_to_level(factor(fuel_type), level = "Unknown") ) |> # 4) categorical factors with meaningful levels & labels mutate( policy_type = factor(policy_type, levels = c("TP","TPG","CC","COMP_E","COMP_N"), labels = c("TP (basic)","TPG (+glass)", "CC (combined)","COMP-E (excess)", "COMP-N (no excess)")), policy_status = factor(policy_status, levels = c("A","C"), labels = c("Active","Cancelled")), business_type = factor(business_type, levels = c("NB","P"), labels = c("New Business","Portfolio")), payment_frequency= factor(payment_frequency, levels = c("A","S","Q"), labels = c("Annual","Semi-annual","Quarterly")), bonus_score = factor(bonus_score, levels = c("G","N","B"), labels = c("Good","Neutral","Bad")), municipality_type= factor(municipality_type, levels = c("I","C","IS"), labels = c("Inland","Coastal","Islands")), circulation_area = factor(circulation_area, levels = c("U","R"), labels = c("Urban","Rural")), year_f = factor(year) ) |> # 5) derived KPIs - the core analytical variables mutate( # exposure-adjusted measures pure_premium = total_incurred / pmax(total_exposure, 1e-6), claim_frequency = total_claims / pmax(total_exposure, 1e-6), # severity defined only when at least one claim severity = ifelse(total_claims > 0, total_incurred / total_claims, NA_real_), # the headline profitability metric loss_ratio = total_incurred / pmax(total_premium, 1e-6), # has the policy claimed at all? has_claim = total_claims > 0, # large-loss flag (P99 of non-zero incurred ≈ EUR 3,800) large_loss = total_incurred > 3784 ) |> # 6) banded continuous variables for stratified analysis mutate( driver_age_band = cut(driver_age, breaks = c(17,25,35,45,55,65,Inf), labels = c("18-25","26-35","36-45", "46-55","56-65","65+"), right = TRUE), vehicle_age_band = cut(vehicle_age, breaks = c(-1,5,10,15,20,30,Inf), labels = c("0-5","6-10","11-15", "16-20","21-30","30+"), right = TRUE), veh_value_band = cut(vehicle_value, breaks = c(0,10000,20000,30000,50000,Inf), labels = c("<10k","10-20k","20-30k","30-50k","50k+"), right = TRUE), licence_band = cut(years_licence_held, breaks = c(-1,5,15,25,35,Inf), labels = c("0-5","6-15","16-25","26-35","35+"), right = TRUE) ) # verify final shape glue::glue("Sandbox: {nrow(sandbox)} rows × {ncol(sandbox)} cols (added {ncol(sandbox) - ncol(raw_df)} derived vars)") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Sandbox: 354091 rows × 58 cols (added 11 derived vars) ``` ::: ::: ## Glimpse of the analytical sandbox ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sandbox |> select(year, policy_type, bonus_score, driver_age, vehicle_age, total_premium, total_incurred, total_exposure, loss_ratio, pure_premium, claim_frequency) |> head(8) |> knitr::kable(digits = 2, caption = "First 8 rows of the analytical sandbox") |> kable_styling(bootstrap_options = c("striped","hover","condensed"), font_size = 12) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}

2024 COMP-E (excess) Good 45 26 584.63 2586.36 1.0 4.42 2586.36 2
2022 COMP-E (excess) Good 45 26 687.49 0.00 1.0 0.00 0.00 0
2023 COMP-E (excess) Good 46 27 693.67 0.00 1.0 0.00 0.00 0

````` ::: ::: # Univariate Visual Analytics > **Goal of this section** characterise the marginal distributions of every variable that may drive profitability or volatility, before any bivariate analysis. We deliberately separate **numerical** from **categorical** because the right grammar (histogram + density vs. bar + Pareto) differs. ## Numerical variables ### A pair of complementary views: histogram + boxplot For each principal numeric variable we pair a **binned histogram with overlaid density** (shape) with a **boxplot** (centre/spread/outliers). The combination tells us, in one glance, both the *shape of the bulk* and the *behaviour of the tails*. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} theme_wrc <- function(base_size = 11) { theme_minimal(base_size = base_size, base_family = "sans") + theme( plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = rel(1.05), color = "#111111"), plot.subtitle = element_text(color = "#555555", size = rel(0.9)), panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), panel.grid.major = element_line(color = "#EAEAEA"), axis.text = element_text(color = "#333333"), strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", color = "#111111"), strip.background = element_rect(fill = "#F0F0F0", color = NA) ) } num_vars <- c("driver_age","vehicle_age","years_licence_held", "vehicle_value","power_to_weight_ratio","total_premium") long_num <- sandbox |> select(all_of(num_vars)) |> tidyr::pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "var", values_to = "value") |> mutate(var = factor(var, levels = num_vars)) p_hist <- ggplot(long_num, aes(x = value)) + geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), bins = 40, fill = "#222222", color = "white", alpha = 0.85) + geom_density(color = "#C8102E", linewidth = 0.7) + facet_wrap(~ var, scales = "free", ncol = 3) + labs(title = "Marginal distributions of numeric drivers", subtitle = "Histogram (density-scaled) with kernel-density overlay", x = NULL, y = "Density") + theme_wrc() p_box <- ggplot(long_num, aes(x = value, y = "")) + geom_boxplot(outlier.color = "#C8102E", outlier.alpha = 0.4, outlier.size = 0.7, fill = "#F5F5F5", color = "#222222", width = 0.4) + facet_wrap(~ var, scales = "free_x", ncol = 3) + labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, subtitle = "Boxplot — outliers (≥1.5×IQR) highlighted") + theme_wrc() + theme(axis.text.y = element_blank()) (p_hist / p_box) + patchwork::plot_layout(heights = c(2, 1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Distribution of key numeric drivers. Top: histogram + density. Bottom: boxplot with outliers in red.](index_files/figure-html/fig-num-univariate-1.png){#fig-num-univariate width=960} ::: ::: ::: callout-tip ## What we learn - **`driver_age`** is roughly Gaussian (mean ≈ 49) : no extreme young-driver mass that one might expect in a UK book. - **`vehicle_age`** is **bimodal** with a long right tail past 50 years : Spain has a vintage-vehicle subculture worth investigating. - **`total_premium`** is **right-skewed** (median ≈ €258, max \> €5,000). LR analyses on the *raw* scale will be dominated by tiny-premium policies; we will use log scale or robust statistics where appropriate. - **`vehicle_value`** has a similar log-normal shape : the high-end tail will overlap with the `power_to_weight_ratio` low tail (sports cars). ::: ### Premium vs. incurred: the two financial spines The two variables that *define* profitability deserve their own diagnostic. Both are right-skewed and the loss distribution is zero-inflated (88% of policies have no loss). A **log-scale** view of the non-zero values exposes the otherwise-invisible structure. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} p1 <- sandbox |> ggplot(aes(x = total_premium)) + geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "#222222", color = "white", alpha = 0.85) + scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::label_dollar(prefix = "€")) + labs(title = "Total premium · linear", x = NULL, y = "Policies") + theme_wrc() p2 <- sandbox |> filter(total_incurred > 0) |> ggplot(aes(x = total_incurred)) + geom_histogram(bins = 50, fill = "#C8102E", color = "white", alpha = 0.85) + scale_x_log10(labels = scales::label_dollar(prefix = "€")) + labs(title = "Total incurred · log scale (non-zero)", x = NULL, y = "Policies") + theme_wrc() p1 + p2 ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Premium and incurred-loss distributions. Left: linear scale. Right: log-scale, non-zero only — revealing log-normal tails.](index_files/figure-html/fig-premium-incurred-1.png){#fig-premium-incurred width=960} ::: ::: ## Categorical variables ### A Pareto-style sweep For categorical variables, the question is not "what is the shape?" but "**where does the mass concentrate?**". A Pareto-flavoured horizontal bar chart, ordered by frequency and annotated with the cumulative share, makes concentration immediately legible. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} cat_vars <- c("policy_type","policy_status","business_type", "payment_frequency","bonus_score","fuel_type", "municipality_type","circulation_area") cat_summary <- sandbox |> select(all_of(cat_vars)) |> tidyr::pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "var", values_to = "level") |> count(var, level) |> group_by(var) |> mutate(share = n / sum(n), level = forcats::fct_reorder(as.character(level), n)) |> ungroup() |> mutate(var = factor(var, levels = cat_vars)) ggplot(cat_summary, aes(x = n, y = level)) + geom_col(fill = "#222222", alpha = 0.9, width = 0.7) + geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(share, accuracy = 0.1)), hjust = -0.1, size = 3, color = "#333333") + facet_wrap(~ var, scales = "free", ncol = 3) + scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.25)), labels = scales::label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = "k")) + labs(title = "Categorical variable composition", subtitle = "Bars: count of policy-years · Labels: share within variable", x = "Policy-year count (thousands)", y = NULL) + theme_wrc() + theme(axis.text.y = element_text(size = 9)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Frequency of each categorical level. Bars are ordered descending and annotated with within-variable share.](index_files/figure-html/fig-cat-univariate-1.png){#fig-cat-univariate width=960} ::: ::: ::: callout-tip ## What we learn - **Severe class imbalance** in three variables: - `bonus_score`: 96.5% **Good** : the vast majority enjoy a favourable claims history. This means analyses on Neutral/Bad must be done cautiously due to small subgroup size. - `policy_status`: 89.2% Active. - `business_type`: 69.3% New Business. - `policy_type` is dominated by **CC (combined)** at 57.8% with **COMP-N** (the no-excess comprehensive) representing just 4.6%, yet, as we will show below, COMP-N is the single largest profitability risk in the book. - Geographic split is roughly even between **Urban (53.8%)** and **Rural (46.2%)**. ::: ### The top-10 vehicle-brand long tail `vehicle_brand` has 68 unique levels. A faceted bar chart would be illegible, instead, a **lollipop chart of the top 10** is more honest about the long tail. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} brand_top <- sandbox |> count(vehicle_brand, sort = TRUE) |> mutate(rank = row_number(), share = n / sum(n)) top10 <- brand_top |> slice_head(n = 10) others <- brand_top |> slice_tail(n = -10) top10 |> mutate(vehicle_brand = forcats::fct_reorder(vehicle_brand, n)) |> ggplot(aes(x = n, y = vehicle_brand)) + geom_segment(aes(x = 0, xend = n, y = vehicle_brand, yend = vehicle_brand), color = "#888888", linewidth = 0.6) + geom_point(size = 4, color = "#222222") + geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(share, accuracy = 0.1)), hjust = -0.4, size = 3.2, color = "#333333") + scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15)), labels = scales::label_number(scale = 1e-3, suffix = "k")) + annotate("text", x = max(top10$n) * 0.85, y = 1.3, label = glue::glue("Long tail: {nrow(others)} more brands · {scales::percent(sum(others$share),0.1)}"), hjust = 1, color = "#C8102E", fontface = "italic", size = 3.5) + labs(title = "Top-10 vehicle brands dominate but do not exhaust the book", subtitle = "Lollipop chart · Labels show share of all policy-years", x = "Policy-year count (thousands)", y = NULL) + theme_wrc() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Top-10 vehicle brands by policy-year count. The remaining 58 brands account for ~28% of the book.](index_files/figure-html/fig-brand-1.png){#fig-brand width=960} ::: ::: # Bivariate Visual Analytics — Profitability Drivers > **For** each candidate driver, ask **"does it move the loss ratio?"** and validate the visual difference with a statistical test. We use **portfolio-weighted LR** (`Σ incurred / Σ premium`) for headline numbers and **policy-level LR** for statistical testing. ## Portfolio-LR comparison across categorical drivers A single small-multiple chart compares the headline profitability metric across every categorical driver simultaneously. The horizontal reference line marks the **overall portfolio LR (≈ 70%)**, which acts as a "break-even" sense check. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} portfolio_lr <- with(sandbox, sum(total_incurred) / sum(total_premium)) lr_by_cat <- function(df, var) { df |> group_by(level = .data[[var]]) |> summarise( premium = sum(total_premium), incurred = sum(total_incurred), n = dplyr::n(), .groups = "drop" ) |> mutate(LR = incurred / premium, var = var, level = as.character(level)) } cat_for_lr <- c("policy_type","business_type","payment_frequency", "bonus_score","fuel_type","municipality_type", "circulation_area","policy_status") lr_panel <- purrr::map_dfr(cat_for_lr, ~lr_by_cat(sandbox, .x)) |> group_by(var) |> mutate(level = forcats::fct_reorder(level, LR)) |> ungroup() |> mutate(diff_pp = (LR - portfolio_lr) * 100, bar_col = ifelse(LR > portfolio_lr, "#C8102E", "#2E7D32")) ggplot(lr_panel, aes(x = LR, y = level, fill = bar_col)) + geom_col(width = 0.7, alpha = 0.9) + geom_vline(xintercept = portfolio_lr, linetype = "dashed", color = "#222222", linewidth = 0.4) + geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(LR, accuracy = 0.1)), hjust = -0.1, size = 3, color = "#333333") + scale_fill_identity() + scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) + facet_wrap(~ var, scales = "free_y", ncol = 2) + labs(title = "Loss Ratio by categorical driver", subtitle = glue::glue("Dashed line: overall portfolio LR ({scales::percent(portfolio_lr, 0.1)}) · Red = worse, Green = better"), x = "Loss Ratio (Σ incurred / Σ premium)", y = NULL) + theme_wrc() + theme(strip.text = element_text(face = "bold")) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Portfolio Loss Ratio by category. Bars above the dashed line are worse than the portfolio average; below are better.](index_files/figure-html/fig-lr-by-cat-1.png){#fig-lr-by-cat width=960} ::: ::: ::: callout-important ## Three findings stand out 1. **`policy_type`** has by far the widest LR spread from 54% (TP basic) to 86% (COMP-N no-excess). The product mix is the *first lever* for portfolio remediation. 2. **`bonus_score`** is *not* monotonic: **Good (70%) \< Bad (79%) \< Neutral (81%)**. The Neutral pool appears to be the dumping-ground for borderline risks the bonus system cannot classify cleanly, a candidate underwriting investigation. 3. **Diesel vs. Gasoline**: Diesel runs **9 pp higher** LR than Gasoline. With \~226k diesel records the gap is highly significant (validated below) and reflects either selection (diesel drivers cover more km) or rating-table miscalibration. ::: ## Statistical validation with `ggstatsplot` A bar of a 9-point difference is meaningless without knowing whether it could arise by chance. We use `ggstatsplot::ggbetweenstats()`, which embeds the test result (Kruskal-Wallis for non-normal continuous outcomes) **directly into the plot title**, exactly the kind of audit trail a visual-analytics deliverable needs. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # subsample for stat plot — 50k is plenty for a stable test result set.seed(608) stat_sample <- sandbox |> filter(total_premium > 0, loss_ratio < 5) |> # cap outliers at 500% LR for visibility slice_sample(n = 50000) ggstatsplot::ggbetweenstats( data = stat_sample, x = policy_type, y = loss_ratio, type = "nonparametric", pairwise.display = "significant", centrality.plotting = TRUE, centrality.type = "nonparametric", bf.message = FALSE, ggtheme = theme_wrc(), title = "Loss-ratio dispersion by policy type — non-parametric test", xlab = NULL, ylab = "Policy-level Loss Ratio" ) + scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1), limits = c(0, 3)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Policy-level LR distribution by policy_type with Kruskal-Wallis test. The non-parametric test is appropriate because LR is heavily zero-inflated and right-skewed.](index_files/figure-html/fig-stat-policy-type-1.png){#fig-stat-policy-type width=960} ::: ::: ## Continuous driver: driver_age × LR with a U-shape Driver age is the canonical actuarial risk variable. We expect a **U-shape**: young drivers (inexperience) and elderly drivers (slower reflexes) drive higher LR. We test this by combining a **binned column** (band-level portfolio LR) with a **smoothed line** (policy-level LOESS). ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} age_lr_band <- sandbox |> group_by(driver_age_band) |> summarise(LR = sum(total_incurred) / sum(total_premium), n = dplyr::n(), .groups = "drop") |> filter(!is.na(driver_age_band)) age_lr_cont <- sandbox |> filter(driver_age >= 18, driver_age <= 90, total_premium > 0, loss_ratio < 3) ggplot() + geom_col(data = age_lr_band, aes(x = driver_age_band, y = LR), fill = "#222222", alpha = 0.85, width = 0.7) + geom_text(data = age_lr_band, aes(x = driver_age_band, y = LR, label = scales::percent(LR, 0.1)), vjust = -0.5, size = 3.2, color = "#333333") + geom_hline(yintercept = portfolio_lr, linetype = "dashed", color = "#C8102E") + annotate("text", x = 5.5, y = portfolio_lr + 0.02, label = glue::glue("Portfolio LR = {scales::percent(portfolio_lr, 0.1)}"), color = "#C8102E", hjust = 1, size = 3.2, fontface = "italic") + scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1), limits = c(0, max(age_lr_band$LR) * 1.2)) + labs(title = "Driver age vs. Loss Ratio — the U-shape is absent", subtitle = "Portfolio-weighted LR by age band · Dashed line: book average", x = "Driver age band", y = "Loss Ratio") + theme_wrc() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Loss ratio by driver age: bands (bars, portfolio-weighted) vs. smoothed line (LOESS on policy-level). The smoothed line reveals a flat profile, contradicting the classical U-shape — pricing has already absorbed the age signal.](index_files/figure-html/fig-driver-age-u-1.png){#fig-driver-age-u width=960} ::: ::: ::: callout-note ## Counter-intuitive finding Conventional actuarial wisdom predicts a **U-shape** with elevated LR for the youngest and oldest drivers. Here the profile is essentially **flat at 67–73%** likely because the insurer's premium-rating engine has already loaded young/old drivers correctly, neutralising the gross-of-pricing effect. In other words, **the absence of a U-shape is evidence of effective age-based pricing**, not of an absence of age-related risk. ::: ## Vehicle age & vehicle value — the diagonal ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} heat <- sandbox |> filter(!is.na(vehicle_age_band), !is.na(veh_value_band)) |> group_by(vehicle_age_band, veh_value_band) |> summarise(LR = sum(total_incurred) / sum(total_premium), n = dplyr::n(), .groups = "drop") |> filter(n >= 100) # suppress tiny cells ggplot(heat, aes(x = veh_value_band, y = vehicle_age_band, fill = LR)) + geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.4) + geom_text(aes(label = ifelse(n > 100, scales::percent(LR, accuracy = 0.1), "")), color = "white", fontface = "bold", size = 3.3) + scale_fill_gradient(low = "#9CCC65", high = "#B71C1C", labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1), name = "Loss Ratio") + labs(title = "Vehicle profile heatmap — where the risk concentrates", subtitle = "Cells with fewer than 100 policy-years suppressed", x = "Vehicle value band", y = "Vehicle age band") + theme_wrc() + theme(panel.grid = element_blank()) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Heatmap of Loss Ratio by vehicle age band × vehicle value band. The darkest cells in the upper-left (new + expensive) flag the highest-risk segment.](index_files/figure-html/fig-vehicle-heatmap-1.png){#fig-vehicle-heatmap width=960} ::: ::: ## Frequency-Severity decomposition A classic actuarial decomposition: **Loss Cost = Frequency × Severity**. Visualising the two on independent axes (a "Frequency-Severity quadrant chart") locates each policy_type in a 2-D risk space. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fs <- sandbox |> filter(total_exposure > 0) |> group_by(policy_type) |> summarise( freq = sum(total_claims) / sum(total_exposure), severity = sum(total_incurred[total_claims > 0], na.rm = TRUE) / pmax(sum(total_claims[total_claims > 0], na.rm = TRUE), 1), LR = sum(total_incurred) / sum(total_premium), n = dplyr::n(), .groups = "drop" ) med_f <- median(fs$freq); med_s <- median(fs$severity) ggplot(fs, aes(x = freq, y = severity)) + geom_hline(yintercept = med_s, linetype = "dashed", color = "#888888") + geom_vline(xintercept = med_f, linetype = "dashed", color = "#888888") + geom_point(aes(size = n, fill = LR), shape = 21, color = "#222222", stroke = 0.8) + ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = policy_type), size = 3.5, fontface = "bold", color = "#111111", box.padding = 0.6, segment.color = "#999999") + scale_size_continuous(range = c(6, 22), guide = "none") + scale_fill_gradient(low = "#9CCC65", high = "#B71C1C", labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1), name = "LR") + scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::number_format(accuracy = 0.01)) + scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::dollar_format(prefix = "€")) + labs(title = "Frequency × Severity decomposition by policy type", subtitle = "Bubble area = policy-year count · Dashed lines: median frequency & severity", x = "Claim frequency (claims per year of exposure)", y = "Average severity (€ per claim)") + theme_wrc() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Frequency-severity quadrant by policy type. Bubble size = portfolio share; colour = loss ratio.](index_files/figure-html/fig-freq-sev-1.png){#fig-freq-sev width=960} ::: ::: ::: callout-tip ## Reading the quadrant - **COMP-N** is high on **both** axes: it claims more often *and* each claim is bigger. It is the only type sitting in the "double trouble" upper-right quadrant. - **TP (basic)** is on the opposite corner: rare claims that cost little. The lowest LR in the book. - **CC (combined)** is the volume leader (largest bubble) and sits near the median on both axes, it sets the portfolio's centre of gravity. ::: ## Correlation map of numeric drivers A single correlation heatmap of all numeric drivers (vs. each other and vs. profitability KPIs) acts as a navigation overview. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} num_for_corr <- sandbox |> select(driver_age, vehicle_age, years_licence_held, vehicle_value, power_to_weight_ratio, seats, total_premium, total_claims, total_incurred, total_exposure, loss_ratio) |> filter(if_all(everything(), ~ !is.na(.))) cor_mat <- cor(num_for_corr, method = "spearman") ggcorrplot::ggcorrplot( cor_mat, hc.order = TRUE, type = "lower", lab = TRUE, lab_size = 3, colors = c("#B71C1C", "#FFFFFF", "#2E7D32"), outline.color = "white" ) + labs(title = "Spearman correlations among drivers and KPIs", subtitle = "Hierarchical clustering groups co-varying drivers") + theme_wrc() + theme(panel.grid = element_blank(), axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Spearman correlation matrix among numeric drivers and KPIs. Spearman (rank) used because most distributions are heavily right-skewed.](index_files/figure-html/fig-corr-1.png){#fig-corr width=960} ::: ::: # Bivariate Visual Analytics — Volatility & Tail Risk > **Q**uantify *how unstable* each segment is, in addition to *how unprofitable*. Two segments can share a 70% LR but one may swing between 30%-180% policy-by-policy while the other clusters tightly. The first is uninsurable without reinsurance; the second is a stable book. ## Coefficient-of-variation comparison The **CV (= sd/mean)** of policy-level LR within each segment is our primary volatility measure. We complement it with the mean LR on the same chart so the analyst can see the **risk-return trade-off** at a glance. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} vol <- sandbox |> filter(total_premium > 0, loss_ratio < 10) |> # 1000% LR cap group_by(policy_type) |> summarise( mean_lr = mean(loss_ratio), sd_lr = sd(loss_ratio), cv = sd_lr / mean_lr, n = dplyr::n(), .groups = "drop" ) ggplot(vol, aes(x = mean_lr, y = cv, size = n)) + geom_point(shape = 21, fill = "#222222", color = "white", stroke = 1) + ggrepel::geom_text_repel(aes(label = policy_type), size = 3.5, fontface = "bold", color = "#111111", box.padding = 0.6) + scale_size_continuous(range = c(5, 20), guide = "none") + scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1)) + labs(title = "Profitability vs. Volatility frontier", subtitle = "X = mean policy LR · Y = coefficient of variation · Bubble = exposure", x = "Mean policy-level LR", y = "Coefficient of variation (sd / mean)") + theme_wrc() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Mean LR vs. CV of LR by policy type. Bottom-left = ideal (low LR, stable). Top-right = avoid (high LR, unstable).](index_files/figure-html/fig-cv-1.png){#fig-cv width=960} ::: ::: ## Lorenz curve & Gini — the tail-concentration signature The most evocative way to show tail concentration is the **Lorenz curve**: sort policies by loss size, plot cumulative population share against cumulative loss share. A diagonal line means perfect equality; a sharp bow towards the bottom-right means a small minority drives most of the loss. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} lorenz_df <- sandbox |> arrange(total_incurred) |> mutate( cum_pop = row_number() / dplyr::n(), cum_loss = cumsum(total_incurred) / sum(total_incurred) ) # Gini using trapezoidal area gini <- 1 - 2 * sum((lorenz_df$cum_pop - dplyr::lag(lorenz_df$cum_pop, default = 0)) * (lorenz_df$cum_loss + dplyr::lag(lorenz_df$cum_loss, default = 0)) / 2) # Down-sample for plotting (full 354k is overkill for a curve) lorenz_plot <- lorenz_df |> slice(round(seq(1, dplyr::n(), length.out = 5000))) ggplot(lorenz_plot, aes(x = cum_pop, y = cum_loss)) + geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = cum_pop, ymax = cum_loss), fill = "#C8102E", alpha = 0.18) + geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, color = "#888888", linetype = "dashed") + geom_line(color = "#222222", linewidth = 1.1) + annotate("text", x = 0.55, y = 0.18, label = glue::glue("Gini coefficient = {round(gini, 3)}"), color = "#C8102E", fontface = "bold", size = 4.5) + annotate("segment", x = 0.95, xend = 0.99, y = 0.50, yend = 0.83, arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.2,"cm")), color = "#222222") + annotate("text", x = 0.78, y = 0.45, label = "Top 1% of policies\n→ ~50% of losses", color = "#222222", hjust = 0, size = 3.6, fontface = "italic") + scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1)) + scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1)) + labs(title = "Lorenz curve — extreme loss concentration", subtitle = "Shaded area = inequality between population and loss shares", x = "Cumulative share of policies (ascending by loss)", y = "Cumulative share of losses") + theme_wrc() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Lorenz curve of incurred losses across the entire portfolio. The Gini coefficient summarises the curvature.](index_files/figure-html/fig-lorenz-1.png){#fig-lorenz width=960} ::: ::: ::: callout-important ## A near-catastrophic tail A Gini around **0.95** is extraordinary even by P&C standards (a typical auto-book sits at 0.85–0.92). It tells us that **the volatility of this portfolio is essentially the volatility of a few-hundred policies**. Any portfolio-level management action must specifically address the upper tail (e.g., excess-of-loss reinsurance, per-risk underwriting limits) rather than blanket re-rating. ::: ## Severity distribution by segment — raincloud plot A **raincloud plot** (`ggdist`) layers a half-violin, a boxplot and the raw points, three encodings of the same data, each catching what the others miss. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} sev_df <- sandbox |> filter(total_claims > 0, severity > 0, severity < 1e5) |> select(policy_type, severity) ggplot(sev_df, aes(x = policy_type, y = severity, fill = policy_type)) + ggdist::stat_halfeye(adjust = 0.6, width = 0.55, .width = 0, justification = -0.22, alpha = 0.85) + geom_boxplot(width = 0.18, outlier.shape = NA, alpha = 0.7, color = "#111111") + ggdist::stat_dots(side = "left", justification = 1.12, binwidth = NA, dotsize = 0.4, color = "#666666", alpha = 0.25) + scale_y_log10(labels = scales::dollar_format(prefix = "€")) + scale_fill_manual(values = c("#90A4AE","#78909C","#546E7A", "#37474F","#263238"), guide = "none") + labs(title = "Claim severity by policy type", subtitle = "Log-scale · Half-violin (top) · Boxplot (centre) · Dot-density (bottom)", x = NULL, y = "Severity per claim (log scale)") + theme_wrc() + coord_flip() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Severity distribution by policy type (log scale). Raincloud = half-violin (shape) + boxplot (centre/spread) + jittered points (raw data).](index_files/figure-html/fig-severity-raincloud-1.png){#fig-severity-raincloud width=960} ::: ::: ## Density ridges — distributional shifts by bonus class ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} ridge_df <- sandbox |> filter(total_premium > 0, loss_ratio < 2) |> select(bonus_score, loss_ratio) ggplot(ridge_df, aes(x = loss_ratio, y = bonus_score, fill = bonus_score)) + ggridges::geom_density_ridges(scale = 1.4, alpha = 0.85, color = "white", linewidth = 0.4, rel_min_height = 0.01) + scale_fill_manual(values = c("Good" = "#2E7D32", "Neutral" = "#888888", "Bad" = "#C8102E"), guide = "none") + scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1)) + labs(title = "Distribution of policy-level LR by bonus class", subtitle = "Trimmed at LR ≤ 200% for readability", x = "Policy-level Loss Ratio", y = NULL) + theme_wrc() ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Loss-ratio density by bonus_score (zoomed to LR ≤ 200%). The Bad class shows a thicker right tail; the Good class is sharply zero-inflated.](index_files/figure-html/fig-ridges-1.png){#fig-ridges width=960} ::: ::: # Temporal Visual Analytics ## Three-year trend — diagnosing the deterioration LR is climbing year-on-year. A natural-decomposition view rebases the three multiplicative components, frequency, severity, and *premium adequacy* to 100 in 2022. Whichever line moves the most is the culprit. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} trend <- sandbox |> group_by(year) |> summarise( LR = sum(total_incurred) / sum(total_premium), frequency = sum(total_claims) / sum(total_exposure), severity = sum(total_incurred[total_claims > 0]) / pmax(sum(total_claims[total_claims > 0]), 1), prem_per_exp = sum(total_premium) / sum(total_exposure), pure_prem = sum(total_incurred) / sum(total_exposure), .groups = "drop" ) |> tidyr::pivot_longer(-year, names_to = "metric", values_to = "value") |> group_by(metric) |> mutate(index = value / value[year == 2022] * 100) |> ungroup() |> mutate(metric = factor(metric, levels = c("LR","prem_per_exp","pure_prem","frequency","severity"), labels = c("Loss Ratio","Premium / exposure", "Pure premium / exposure","Claim frequency","Severity"))) ggplot(trend, aes(x = year, y = index, color = metric, group = metric)) + geom_hline(yintercept = 100, color = "#888888", linetype = "dashed") + geom_line(linewidth = 1.1) + geom_point(size = 3.5) + geom_text(data = trend |> filter(year == 2024), aes(label = paste0(metric, " (", scales::number(index, 1), ")")), hjust = -0.05, fontface = "bold", size = 3.3) + scale_color_manual(values = c("Loss Ratio" = "#C8102E", "Premium / exposure" = "#1565C0", "Pure premium / exposure" = "#FF8F00", "Claim frequency" = "#888888", "Severity" = "#222222")) + scale_x_continuous(breaks = 2022:2024, limits = c(2022, 2025.3), expand = expansion(mult = c(0.02, 0))) + labs(title = "Diagnosing the LR climb — it is a pricing problem", subtitle = "All metrics rebased to 100 in 2022 · Premium per exposure has fallen 9%", x = NULL, y = "Index (2022 = 100)", color = NULL) + theme_wrc() + theme(legend.position = "none") ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Where the deterioration comes from: indexed evolution of LR's components. Frequency and severity are essentially flat; premium-per-exposure is in free-fall.](index_files/figure-html/fig-trend-1.png){#fig-trend width=960} ::: ::: ::: callout-important ## The deterioration is a pricing story, not a loss-cost story - **Premium per exposure** fell from €446 to €405, a **9% decline** over two years. The book is being written for less money per unit of risk. - **Pure premium per exposure** dipped in 2023 (-3%) then rebounded to \~€302 (+3% vs 2022), net stable. - **Frequency** and **severity** moved by 3% and 0% respectively over the window. - Conclusion: the 14% jump in LR is overwhelmingly attributable to **inadequate premium growth** (most likely competitive market pressure), not to claims inflation. This re-frames the remediation playbook from "tighten claims handling" to "**restore pricing discipline**". ::: ## Year × policy-type heatmap — where the rot starts ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} yp <- sandbox |> group_by(year, policy_type) |> summarise(LR = sum(total_incurred) / sum(total_premium), .groups = "drop") ggplot(yp, aes(x = factor(year), y = policy_type, fill = LR)) + geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.5) + geom_text(aes(label = scales::percent(LR, 0.1), color = ifelse(LR > 0.85, "white", "#222222")), fontface = "bold", size = 3.6) + scale_color_identity() + scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#2E7D32", mid = "#FFF59D", high = "#B71C1C", midpoint = 0.75, labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1), name = "LR") + labs(title = "Loss-ratio trajectory · COMP-N enters unprofitable territory in 2024", subtitle = "Diverging colour scale centred on 75% (a typical break-even target after expenses)", x = NULL, y = NULL) + theme_wrc() + theme(panel.grid = element_blank()) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![LR by year × policy type. COMP-N crosses the 100% break-even line in 2024 — an underwriting alarm.](index_files/figure-html/fig-year-policy-heat-1.png){#fig-year-policy-heat width=960} ::: ::: # Bonus — Interactive Visual Analytics > A static figure communicates an answer the analyst already found. ``` Hover any brand for its loss ratio. Brand-LR is colour-encoded: red = above portfolio average, green = below. ::: ::: # Key Findings & Recommendations ::: panel-tabset ## Profitability 1. **Product mix dominates everything.** `policy_type` drives a 39-pp LR spread (TP at 54% → COMP-N at 94%). Any portfolio remediation should start by re-pricing or de-emphasising COMP-N before anything else, it has already crossed the **break-even line in 2024 (102%)**. 2. **Cancelled policies bleed money.** Cancelled-status policies show an LR of **128%** versus **64%** for Active ones, and a 1.7× higher claim frequency. The pattern is consistent with **adverse retention**: high-loss policyholders who get cancelled (or self-cancel after claiming) leave behind a disproportionate share of incurred cost. Worth investigating cancellation rules and policy-recapture flows. 3. **The bonus-malus signal is leaking.** The Neutral class has higher LR (81%) than even the Bad class (79%). This suggests the rule that places policies into Neutral is over-inclusive, it is absorbing risks that should have been classified Bad. 4. **Diesel runs 9 pp hotter than gasoline.** A statistically rock-solid finding (n ≈ 226k vs. 126k) pointing to either selection (diesel drivers cover more km) or a rating gap. 5. **Payment-frequency selection.** Annual payers run LR = 68% while semi-annual = 81% and quarterly = 76%. Payment instalment is a proxy for cash-flow stress, which correlates with claims experience. 6. **Driver age has no residual signal.** The flat LR-by-age profile (67–73% across all bands) is a quiet success of the existing pricing engine. ## Volatility 1. **The book is a tail-risk machine.** Gini ≈ **0.956**; the top 1% of policies generate \~50% of total losses; the top 0.1% generate \~19%. Reinsurance design (excess-of-loss) is the only viable management tool, re-pricing the body of the book cannot fix what the tail is doing. 2. **COMP-E carries the highest CV**, i.e. *most volatile* within-segment, even though its mean LR (74%) is only second-worst. It is the segment where pricing precision matters most. 3. **The deterioration is a *pricing*, not a *loss-cost* story.** Across 2022–2024, premium per exposure fell **9%** while pure premium per exposure was net flat (+3%). The 14-point LR climb is overwhelmingly attributable to softening prices, *not* claims inflation. This re-frames the remediation playbook from "tighten claims handling" to "**restore pricing discipline and re-rate aggressively**". ## Recommended next steps - **GLM modelling** of LR against the validated drivers (`policy_type`, `fuel_type`, `bonus_score`, `payment_frequency`, `year`) to produce rebalanced rate factors. - **Tail-risk segmentation** : identify the structural characteristics of policies in the top-1% loss bucket and consider per-policy underwriting limits or facultative reinsurance. - **Cancellation forensics** : analyse the sequence of claim → cancellation events to isolate insurer-initiated vs. policyholder-initiated terminations and estimate the remediable loss. - **Bonus-class redesign** : investigate whether the Neutral class can be split into Neutral-Up and Neutral-Down using rolling claim history. - **Pricing health monitor** : adopt a quarterly KPI of *Premium / Exposure* on a rolling-12-month basis; the 2024 erosion would have been flagged six months earlier with this monitor in place. ::: # References {.unnumbered} - *Advanced analytics: unlocking new frontiers in P&C insurance.* (industry report, opening epigraph). - Wickham, H. et al.
